books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: John C. Calhoun, speech on the slavery question, read in the Senate by James M. Mason, March 4, 1850

stimulus.source_note: John C. Calhoun, speech on the slavery question, read in the Senate by Senator James M. Mason, March 4, 1850 (Congressional Globe, 31st Congress, 1st session). Public domain.
stimulus.text:
I have, Senators, believed from the first that the agitation of the subject of slavery would, if not prevented by some timely and effective measure, end in disunion.

. . .

You have thus had forced upon you the greatest and the gravest question that can ever come under your consideration: How can the Union be preserved?

. . .

To this question there can be but one answer, — that the immediate cause is the almost universal discontent which pervades all the States composing the Southern section of the Union.

. . .

It is a great mistake to suppose that disunion can be effected by a single blow. The cords which bind these States together in one common Union are far too numerous and powerful for that. Disunion must be the work of time.

. . .

I return to the question with which I commenced, How can the Union be saved? There is but one way by which it can with any certainty; and that is, by a full and final settlement, on the principle of justice, of all the questions at issue between the two sections.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Calhoun argues that the Union can be saved only by

options.text: admitting California at once and banning slavery in the territories.
options.misconception: Background from the books: Calhoun opposed admitting California as a free state; his speech demands a settlement that satisfies the South, not a Northern victory.

options.text: letting the Supreme Court settle every question about slavery.
options.misconception: The courts play no part in Calhoun's remedy; he calls for a political settlement between the sections.

options.text: a full and final settlement of all questions between the sections.
a constitutional amendment abolishing slavery gradually.
options.misconception: Background from the books: Calhoun was slavery's leading defender in the Senate, and his speech demands a settlement that satisfies the South; gradual abolition is the opposite of his position.

rationales.A: Background from the books: Calhoun opposed admitting California as a free state; his speech demands a settlement that satisfies the South, not a Northern victory.
rationales.B: The courts play no part in Calhoun's remedy; he calls for a political settlement between the sections.
rationales.C: Calhoun's answer is exact: “a full and final settlement, on the principle of justice, of all the questions at issue between the two sections.”
rationales.D: Background from the books: Calhoun was slavery's leading defender in the Senate, and his speech demands a settlement that satisfies the South; gradual abolition is the opposite of his position.
rationales.general:
1. Follow Calhoun's own chain: first the danger, then the question of how the Union can be saved.
2. Hear his one answer: a settlement, full and final, on the principle of justice.
3. Notice the two words that do the work: “full” means every question, and “final” means settled for good.
Remember: when a speaker demands a “final settlement,” he is saying half-measures will not hold.
